subject: Packrat downloads wrong version of caret package.

messages.author: fec70e36c14a7891
messages.subject: Packrat downloads wrong version of caret package.
parts:
Hi Kevin,

Thanks for fixing the problems that were vexing me previously. I've got a new one. When I run packrat:::init() on a new project it installs a version of caret that I don't even have installed on my computer. How is that?

I'm trying to run an older version of caret (caret_6.0-22), but it packrat installs the latest version (caret_6.0-35), which causes my code to fail. Any thoughts on how this could be happening?

Thanks,
Jeff

messages.author: ab0d2be2ea8dabe8
messages.subject: Re: Packrat downloads wrong version of caret package.
parts:
Hi Jeff,

On initialization, packrat will attempt to install the exact version of the package on your system if possible, and fall 'back' to the latest CRAN version if for some reason it does not know how to retrieve that version.

How was the older version of caret installed? If you had installed it from source without letting packrat know how to retrieve it, that could be the cause of the problem.

Can you give the output of:

    readLines(system.file("DESCRIPTION", package = "caret"))

in a non-packrat R session?

You _should_ be able to resolve this by explicitly installing an older version of caret from the CRAN archives: http://cran.us.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/caret/caret_6.0-22.tar.gz (packrat will then track that version).

If the version of `caret` you have installed still has:

    Repository: CRAN

in the DESCRIPTION, then this may be a packrat bug.

Thanks,
Kevin

messages.author: fec70e36c14a7891
messages.subject: Re: Packrat downloads wrong version of caret package.
parts:
Hi Kevin,

I had an exchange with Max Kuhn, the author of the caret package. I had been having trouble running my my code with the current version of caret when using packrat. It turns out that packrat wasn't installing all of caret's suggested dependencies. Specifically, it wasn't installing the e1071 package, which was required for the analysis I was running. I was able to resolve this by adding a line library(e1071) to my script, which prompted packrat to install it. Normally caret loads and installs it internally.

I'll paste my exchange with Max below, where he indicates that he changed how caret handles dependencies.

Best,
Jeff

\\..//..\\..//..\\..//..\\..//..\\..//..\\..//..\\..//..\\..//..\\..//..\\..//..\\..//..\\..//..\\..//..\\..//..\\..//..
On 10/9/2014 9:03 AM, Jeffrey Evans wrote:

I think that was it Max. After I sent that message to you I ran install.packages("e1071") and caret worked.
The problem only came up when using packrat to share and manage packages. It must have a preference for curating a more limited suite of packages.

Thanks again!
Jeff

On 10/9/2014 8:18 AM, Kuhn, Max wrote:
Sort of. I changes how package dependencies are handled. With the previous version, it probably would have installed e1071. Try using install.packages(, dependencies = c(“Depends”, “Suggests”))

Max

From: Jeffrey Evans
Date: Wednesday, October 8, 2014 at 4:11 PM
To: Max
Subject: Re: warning in caret?

I have another for you.

What changed between versions 6.0-22 and the current 6.0-35 that would cause an error when I try to fit a categorical in rpart? This code ran in the old version where yvar (the response) is a factor. 

> yvar = factor(dat$prop.res.plt>0)
>         xvars=c(mgtVars)
>         c.dat=dat[,xvars]
>         repeats=30
>         tuneLength=(length(xvars))-1
>         weights=dat$data.years
>         idx = dat$mgt.data=="yes" & dat$data.years>2
> >   
>   if (is.null(idx)){
+     idx = rep(T,length(yvar))
+   }
>   if (!is.null(weights)){
+     weights = weights[idx]
+   }
>   
>   # bind the dependent and independent variables
>   c.dat = cbind(yvar,c.dat[,xvars])[idx,]
>     
>   # set training controls 
>   # use the oneSE method described in Venables and Ripley (2002) chapter 9 to prune the final model.
>   tc <- trainControl("repeatedcv", repeats=repeats, selectionFunction="oneSE",
+                      returnData=FALSE,num=10)
>   
>   # run the model
>   mod <- train(yvar ~ ., data=c.dat, method="rpart", trControl=tc,
+                na.action=na.rpart,
+                weights=weights,
+                tuneLength=tuneLength,
+                control=rpart.control(usesurrogate=0))
Loading required namespace: e1071
Error in loadNamespace(name) : there is no package called ‘e1071’

Thanks again,
Jeff

messages.author: ab0d2be2ea8dabe8
messages.subject: Re: Packrat downloads wrong version of caret package.
parts:
Hi Jeff,

The issue here is that 'e1071' is a suggested package for caret (it lives in 'Suggests:') and by default packrat does not install packages in Suggests: (since they should not be necessary for 'normal' package function).

In this case, the onus is on the user to explicitly install any packages in Suggests: that may be required -- in this case the error message would have been very helpful, since it's essentially saying "I'm trying to use something from the 'e1071' package, but it doesn't exist".

Note that packrat will track any manually installed packages as well (and will begin snapshotting them after you've explicitly installed it), so after installing `e1071` in your packrat project manually you should be good to go.

In my humble opinion -- if `caret` requires `e1071` to function normally, then `e1071` should be in the `Imports:` set of packages for `caret`.

Thanks,
Kevin

May I ask a simple question about distributing a packrat project? I want to share my project code as an online supplement to a scientific paper. Best,

messages.author: ab0d2be2ea8dabe8
messages.subject: Re: Packrat downloads wrong version of caret package.
parts:
My main suggestion would be to host your project publicly with e.g. GitHub -- then users who want to replicate your analysis and just clone that repository, restore the packrat library, and then re-run any analysis scripts.

We typically suggest sharing:

1. The project files themselves,
2. The packrat lock file,
3. The packrat project options,
4. (optionally, but recommended) the package souce tarballs.

Bundling the package sources should be optional -- as long as packrat knows how to retrieve them online, it can do so, but to be safe you may prefer bundling the tarballs (so one could restore a project with e.g. no internet access).

Sharing the packrat library isn't required (and is probably a bad idea -- it's best to rebuild packages from source on new machines as necessary).

If you just want to share a zip file (tarball) of your project, you can use `packrat::bundle()` as well.
